metadata.title: Half Guard Pass | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Half Guard Pass position in BJJ. Complete guide covering passing mechanics, knee slice, underhook control, and submissions. Offensive 3-point position with 70% pass rate.

overview:
Half Guard Pass represents the critical transitional state where the top player is actively working to complete their guard pass against bottom player's half guard retention. This position exists in the dynamic space between being controlled in half guard and achieving full side control or mount. The top player has cleared one leg but the bottom player maintains control of the other leg with their half guard, creating a strategic battleground where timing, pressure, and technical precision determine the outcome.

From a systematic perspective, the half guard pass position requires the top player to address multiple defensive layers: the bottom player's leg entanglement, their upper body frames, and their ability to recover full guard or initiate sweeps. Success in this position depends on controlling the bottom player's inside space, preventing underhook acquisition, and maintaining forward pressure while methodically extracting the trapped leg. The position is characterized by constant micro-adjustments as both players fight for positional advantages that can shift the momentum dramatically.

This transitional position is one of the highest-leverage areas in BJJ, as completing the pass yields 3 points in competition and establishes dominant control. The half guard pass requires practitioners to develop a systematic approach that addresses common defensive structures (knee shield, lockdown, deep half) while maintaining offensive pressure. Advanced players use this position to set up submission threats that accelerate the passing process, creating dilemmas where the bottom player must choose between defending the pass or defending the submission, often compromising both.

Bottom player maintains some form of leg entanglement on top player's trapped leg (standard half, knee shield, lockdown, or deep half configuration) while attempting to establish frames, underhooks, or recovery pathways
Top player's trapped leg remains controlled but not fully compromised, allowing continued forward pressure and passing attempts while managing bottom player's retention efforts and sweep threats

Control the inside space by keeping chest tight to opponent's torso, eliminating frames and underhook opportunities
Secure crossface or head control to limit bottom player's mobility and ability to turn into you
Keep weight distributed forward onto opponent's chest while maintaining base with free leg

common_errors.error: Allowing bottom player to establish strong underhook on trapped leg side
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player gains leverage for sweeps, can recover guard structure, and controls passing angles
common_errors.correction: Fight for inside position immediately with tight crossface, block underhook attempt with your own underhook or whizzer, maintain chest pressure to prevent space for arm insertion

common_errors.error: Bringing weight too far back or sitting upright
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player creates space to recover full guard, insert knee shield, or initiate sweep attempts
common_errors.correction: Keep chest pressure forward and low, hips driving toward opponent's head, maintain constant downward pressure to prevent space creation

common_errors.error: Neglecting head control or crossface
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player maintains mobility to turn into you, establish frames, create recovery angles, or threaten sweeps
common_errors.correction: Secure crossface immediately by driving forearm across face toward far shoulder, or control head with hand grip, limiting bottom player's ability to turn or bridge

common_errors.error: Poor base with free leg allowing it to be too close or too extended
common_errors.consequence: Vulnerable to sweep attempts, off-balancing, or inability to generate passing pressure
common_errors.correction: Position free leg at optimal distance (typically knee at hip level), maintaining strong base while allowing hip pressure forward, adjust base dynamically based on bottom player's movements

common_errors.error: Rushing the pass without addressing defensive layers systematically
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player maintains retention mechanisms (knee shield, underhook, frames), pass is blocked or reversed
common_errors.correction: Follow systematic sequence: establish crossface, prevent underhook, clear knee shield or frames, control hips, then extract leg and complete pass

common_errors.error: Allowing bottom player to turn to their side and establish strong frames
common_errors.consequence: Creates defensive structure that is difficult to pass, enables guard recovery and sweep opportunities
common_errors.correction: Keep bottom player's shoulders flat to mat with chest pressure, attack underhook side proactively, use weight distribution to prevent turning

common_errors.error: Gripping without purpose or maintaining static grips
common_errors.consequence: Energy waste, telegraphs intentions, allows bottom player to counter-grip effectively
common_errors.correction: Use grips actively to control specific threats (prevent underhook, control knee shield), break grips that give bottom player advantages, transition grips as you progress through passing sequence

training_drills.name: Half Guard Pass Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Start in half guard pass position with training partner providing progressive resistance. Practice transitioning between different passing approaches (knee slice, crossface, underhook) based on partner's defensive reactions. Focus on maintaining pressure and connection throughout transitions. Partner gradually increases resistance from 30% to 70%.

training_drills.name: Crossface and Head Control Maintenance
training_drills.description: Positional sparring starting from half guard pass with emphasis on maintaining crossface or head control. Top player must keep crossface secure while bottom player attempts to clear it and establish underhook. Reset when crossface is lost or pass is completed. Develops sensitivity to head control details and pressure application.

training_drills.name: Systematic Passing Sequence
training_drills.description: Bottom player presents specific defensive structures (knee shield, lockdown, deep half threat) in rotation. Top player must identify the structure and execute appropriate passing sequence. Focus on recognizing defensive patterns and applying systematic solutions. Includes: establish crossface, prevent underhook, clear shield, extract leg, secure side control.

training_drills.name: Submission Setup from Half Guard Pass
training_drills.description: Positional drill where top player practices setting up submissions (kimura, darce) from half guard pass position when bottom player makes specific errors (overcommits to underhook, turns away). Bottom player provides resistance but occasionally presents submission opportunities. Develops ability to recognize and capitalize on submission openings during passing.

training_drills.name: Live Half Guard Passing Rounds
training_drills.description: Full resistance positional sparring starting from half guard pass position. Top player works to complete pass within time limit while bottom player defends, sweeps, or recovers guard. Reset to starting position after each successful outcome. Track success rates to monitor technical development over time.

expert_insights.danaher: The half guard pass represents one of the most technically demanding positions in ground fighting because it requires simultaneous management of multiple defensive systems while maintaining offensive pressure. The fundamental mechanical problem is that you must extract your trapped leg while preventing the bottom player from using that same leg as a lever for sweeps or guard recovery. The solution lies in understanding that passing half guard is not a single technique but a systematic progression through defensive layers. First, you must establish head control or a crossface to limit the bottom player's mobility and prevent them from turning into you effectively. Second, you must control the inside space by preventing the underhook, as this is the bottom player's primary offensive weapon from half guard. Third, you must address their leg configuration, whether it's a knee shield, lockdown, or standard half guard structure. Only after systematically dismantling these defensive layers can you safely extract your leg and complete the pass. The practitioners who excel at passing half guard understand that pressure is not merely about weight distribution but about creating a constant forward vector that denies the bottom player the ability to create recovery angles. Your hips must perpetually drive toward their head while your upper body controls their ability to turn or frame effectively.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Half guard passing is where matches are won or lost at the highest levels because everyone has a half guard game now. The key insight from competition is that you can't just power through good half guard retention, you need to create dilemmas. When I'm passing half guard, I'm immediately looking for the kimura grip on their underhook attempt because that's what everyone wants. Once they commit to that underhook, their arm is exposed and now they have to choose between defending the kimura or defending the pass, and usually they can't do both effectively. The crossface is absolutely critical, but it's not just about pushing their head away. You want to use the crossface to control their entire upper body rotation and create angles where they can't effectively use their frames. In competition, I've found that the knee slice is the highest percentage finish from half guard pass, but you have to set it up by first threatening other passes or submissions. If they're worried about a kimura or a darce setup, the knee slice becomes much easier because their defensive attention is divided. The other critical detail is pace. You can't give them time to establish their full defensive structure. You need to be constantly progressing, constantly attacking, forcing them to defend multiple threats simultaneously until something breaks down.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Half guard passing is all about understanding the game they're trying to play from bottom and shutting it down before it starts. From the 10th Planet perspective, we see so many different half guard variations—lockdown, electric chair setups, old school sweeps, deep half entries—and the key is recognizing what system they're trying to implement and attacking it early. When someone's playing lockdown, they want you to stay heavy and static so they can break you down and create sweep angles. The counter is to stay mobile, keep your weight shifting, and attack their lockdown with specific breaks while threatening submissions that make them choose between the sweep and defending their neck or arm. The crossface is crucial, but I also love the gift wrap from half guard pass when they're fighting for that underhook. You can wrap their arm up and take away their primary offensive tool while setting up devastating back takes or submissions. The other thing about half guard passing is that you should never be just passing—you should be threatening. Every passing attempt should have a submission component to it. Are you threatening a darce? A kimura? An arm crush? When you make passing and submission one combined attack, their defense becomes much more difficult because they can't focus entirely on retention. The modern game requires you to be fluid between passing systems. If the knee slice isn't there, can you transition to a long step? Can you go to a smash pass? That versatility and creativity in your passing game is what makes you unpredictable and ultimately successful.

overview:
Half Guard Pass Position is the advantageous top position where you are working to pass your opponent's half guard. One of your legs is trapped between your opponent's legs, but you have established upper body control and are positioned to complete the pass to side control or mount. This is a critical juncture in BJJ where the battle between guard retention and passing is intensely contested.

From this position, you have earned partial control and points in most rule sets, but full passing requires freeing your trapped leg and establishing complete side control or mount. Success requires combining pressure, proper weight distribution, and systematic passing techniques while defending against sweeps and submissions from the bottom player.

The half guard pass position represents a transitional state where technical precision and patience are paramount. Rushing the pass often leads to sweeps or deeper half guard entries, while methodical pressure and systematic leg extraction create high-percentage passing opportunities. Understanding the opponent's defensive frames, underhook battles, and knee shield variations is essential for successful navigation of this position.
state_invariants: One of your legs is trapped between opponent's legs in half guard configuration, with their inside leg controlling your knee line and their outside leg hooking around your trapped leg
Your chest, shoulder, or upper body is applying downward pressure on opponent's torso, preventing them from creating space or establishing strong frames
Your free leg is positioned outside opponent's body providing base, posting ability, and driving power for passing attempts
prerequisites: Understanding of pressure passing principles and weight distribution
Knowledge of half guard dynamics from both top and bottom perspectives
Upper body control techniques including crossface, underhook, and head positioning
Balance and base fundamentals with ability to maintain stability while one leg is trapped
Recognition of common half guard variations including knee shield, lockdown, and deep half entries
key_principles: Pressure and Weight Distribution: Apply constant chest and shoulder pressure to flatten opponent and limit their mobility
Underhook Control: Secure underhooks to control opponent's upper body, prevent their offensive options, and facilitate passing
Crossface Application: Use crossface to turn opponent's head away, flatten them to their back, and break their defensive structure
Leg Extraction: Systematically work to free trapped leg while maintaining upper body control and pressure
Base with Free Leg: Use free leg for stability, driving power, and directional changes during passing attempts
Head Position: Keep head tight to opponent to prevent them from creating frames or establishing distance
Patience and Pressure: Avoid rushing the pass, instead using sustained pressure to tire opponent and create passing opportunities

common_errors.error: Rushing the leg extraction without establishing upper body control first
common_errors.consequence: Leaves you off-balance and vulnerable to sweeps, deep half guard entries, or lockdown control
common_errors.correction: Establish solid upper body control with crossface or underhook, apply sustained pressure to flatten opponent, then systematically work to free trapped leg while maintaining control

common_errors.error: Insufficient pressure application allowing opponent to create space and frames
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can establish knee shield, create distance, and maintain half guard retention indefinitely
common_errors.correction: Keep chest and shoulder pressure constant, drive weight through opponent's diaphragm, and eliminate any space between your torso and theirs

common_errors.error: Posting with both hands creating space between chest and opponent
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can bridge, create frames, and potentially sweep or recover full guard
common_errors.correction: Keep at least one point of contact with chest or shoulder on opponent, use hands for control rather than posting when possible

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to secure strong underhook on trapped leg side
common_errors.consequence: Opponent gains leverage for sweeps and can come to knees or enter deep half guard
common_errors.correction: Fight for underhook control yourself, use whizzer or crossface to prevent opponent's underhook, maintain head position tight to their body

common_errors.error: Ignoring opponent's lockdown or deep half guard setup
common_errors.consequence: Gets trapped in lockdown limiting mobility or pulled into deep half guard where opponent has strong sweeping options
common_errors.correction: Monitor opponent's leg hooks constantly, adjust base and posture when they attempt lockdown, be prepared to switch passing angles if deep half threat emerges

common_errors.error: Using only strength and pressure without technical leg extraction sequence
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy, allows opponent to rest and defend indefinitely, may lead to stalling calls in competition
common_errors.correction: Learn systematic leg extraction techniques, combine pressure with technical movements, use opponent's defensive reactions to create passing opportunities

common_errors.error: Leaving trapped leg extended rather than keeping knee bent and protected
common_errors.consequence: Vulnerable to kneebar attacks and leg entanglement submissions
common_errors.correction: Keep trapped leg's knee bent and close to opponent's body, monitor for leg attack setups, be ready to defend or extract if submission threat appears

expert_insights.danaher: The half guard pass position represents a critical decision point in the grappling exchange where systematic technical precision vastly outperforms explosive athleticism. The fundamental principle governing successful half guard passing is the establishment of superior upper body control before attempting leg extraction. Your crossface, underhook, or head position must first neutralize the opponent's offensive potential from bottom half guard. Only then can you safely work to free your trapped leg. The common error of rushing the leg extraction stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of positional hierarchy - upper body control precedes lower body advancement. Additionally, the concept of pressure distribution is paramount: your chest and shoulder pressure must be constant and directed through the opponent's diaphragm, not merely resting on their torso. This creates a cumulative fatigue effect that systematically degrades their defensive capacity over time, making the actual pass technically easier as the exchange progresses.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, half guard passing is where matches are won and lost, and I've found that patience combined with relentless pressure is the winning formula. When I'm in half guard top, I'm not thinking about passing immediately - I'm thinking about making my opponent so uncomfortable that they make mistakes trying to escape the pressure. My chest and shoulder pressure needs to be suffocating, literally making it difficult for them to breathe normally. This creates desperation, and desperation creates errors. The knee slice is my highest percentage pass from here because it's both offensive and defensive - as I'm passing, I'm also preventing them from coming to their knees or entering deep half. One key detail that most people miss: when you have the underhook, your elbow must stay tight to your ribs and your forearm must drive across their chest, not just hold loosely. This connection prevents them from turning into you and creates the pathway for your pass. If they start setting up lockdown or deep half, I immediately switch my base and sometimes even change passing directions completely rather than fighting through their strongest defensive position.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: From the 10th Planet perspective, we're hyper-aware of lockdown, deep half, and electric chair setups when someone is in our half guard, so when I'm on top, I'm constantly monitoring for these same threats. The key is recognizing the early warning signs - if they're trying to get their bottom leg across your hip or diving for your far knee, they're setting up deep half. If they're trying to close their legs around your trapped leg, lockdown is coming. The moment I sense these setups, I change the game completely. Sometimes I'll actually give them a different problem to solve by switching to a different passing angle or even momentarily releasing pressure to reset in a better position. The whizzer becomes super important against half guard players who like to come to their knees because it shuts down their entire sweeping game. One unconventional approach we use is actually encouraging them into certain defensive positions that we have specific passing sequences for - it's like chess where you give them moves that look good but actually play into your strategy. And never underestimate the power of good old-fashioned shoulder pressure and crossface - some of the simplest techniques are the most effective when applied with proper mechanics and relentless commitment.

overview:
Half Guard Pass Top Position represents the transitional control state where the top practitioner is actively working to overcome the bottom player's half guard retention while maintaining dominant positioning. This position is characterized by the top player having established positional control elements (underhooks, crossface, knee placement) while the bottom player still retains one leg trapped between their legs. The half guard pass is one of the most fundamental and frequently encountered positions in modern BJJ, as half guard has become a primary retention and recovery position for bottom players. Success in this position requires understanding pressure distribution, base management, and the ability to neutralize the bottom player's retention frames while systematically removing their defensive structures. The position exists in a dynamic tension where the bottom player fights to retain guard or sweep while the top player works methodically to complete the pass to side control, mount, or other dominant positions.

From a strategic perspective, the Half Guard Pass Top Position requires patience and systematic pressure rather than explosive movements. Top players must establish control of the upper body (typically through underhook control and crossface pressure) while simultaneously addressing the bottom player's knee shield, underhooks, or lockdown. The key principle is creating immobility in the bottom player's hips and shoulders before attempting the final pass. Elite passers understand that rushing the pass often results in sweeps or scrambles, while methodical pressure and proper sequencing lead to high-percentage completions. The position also serves as a gateway to various submission opportunities (kimuras, darces, guillotines) when the bottom player creates defensive reactions.

The modern evolution of half guard passing has moved toward smash-passing techniques, headquarters positioning, and leg weave controls that neutralize the bottom player's ability to create angles or recover full guard. Understanding the decision tree of when to apply crushing pressure versus when to use mobility and backstep passes is essential for developing a complete half guard passing game that works against all levels of opposition.

common_errors.error: Allowing bottom player to establish underhook without immediately countering
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player gains sweep opportunities and can recover to better positions like dogfight or full guard
common_errors.correction: Fight aggressively for underhook control from the start, or immediately attack with kimura when opponent gets underhook

common_errors.error: Keeping hips too high or creating space between chest and opponent
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can shrimp, recover guard, or establish frames that prevent pass completion
common_errors.correction: Drive chest pressure downward and keep hips low and heavy on opponent's hip and torso

common_errors.error: Rushing the pass before removing defensive structures
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player sweeps or recovers guard because their frames and hooks are still functional
common_errors.correction: Systematically remove knee shield, underhooks, and other defenses before attempting final pass

common_errors.error: Posting hands too far away from opponent's body
common_errors.consequence: Creates gaps that allow hip escapes, reduces pressure, and makes sweeps easier
common_errors.correction: Keep hands close to opponent's body, using crossface and underhook positions rather than wide posts

common_errors.error: Ignoring the trapped leg and allowing lockdown establishment
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player gains significant control and can execute lockdown-based sweeps and attacks
common_errors.correction: Keep trapped leg mobile, create tension away from lockdown position, or immediately address lockdown before it's fully locked

common_errors.error: Failing to control bottom player's head and shoulder alignment
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can turn into you, create angles, and establish better defensive or offensive positions
common_errors.correction: Use crossface or head control to pin shoulder to mat and prevent opponent from turning

common_errors.error: Using only upper body pressure without engaging hips and legs
common_errors.consequence: Unstable base that's vulnerable to sweeps, insufficient pressure to flatten opponent
common_errors.correction: Integrate whole-body pressure using hips, chest, and strategic leg positioning for maximum control

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Half Guard Pass
training_drills.description: Start in half guard pass position with bottom player having half guard retention. Top player works to pass within 2 minutes while bottom player defends and attempts sweeps. Reset and switch roles. Focus on maintaining pressure, removing defensive structures systematically, and completing passes.

training_drills.name: Progressive Resistance Half Guard Passing
training_drills.description: Bottom player provides 25%, 50%, then 75% resistance over three rounds. Top player practices different passing sequences (smash, knee slice, long step, headquarters) against increasing resistance. Emphasize proper technique at lower resistance before adding intensity.

training_drills.name: Half Guard Pass to Submission Chains
training_drills.description: Flow drill where top player attempts pass and bottom player defends. When bottom player creates specific defensive reactions (underhook, turn away, frame), top player immediately transitions to appropriate submission (kimura, darce, anaconda). Practice recognizing triggers and smooth transitions.

training_drills.name: Headquarters Position Retention
training_drills.description: Establish headquarters position with knee shield smashed and crossface control. Bottom player attempts to recover half guard or sweep while top player maintains position for 30-second intervals. Focus on hip pressure, crossface maintenance, and base stability.

training_drills.name: Underhook Battle Drill
training_drills.description: Start in neutral half guard position. Both players fight for underhook control. Winner must maintain underhook while advancing position (pass if top, sweep if bottom). Emphasizes the critical importance of underhook in half guard dynamics.

expert_insights.danaher: The half guard pass represents a critical juncture where theoretical understanding of positional hierarchy meets practical application of pressure and control mechanics. The fundamental principle that governs success in this position is the systematic dismantling of the opponent's defensive structure before attempting the final pass. Most practitioners fail because they attempt to pass while the bottom player still has functional frames, underhooks, or knee shields in place. The correct approach is to view half guard passing as a sequential problem: first, establish upper body control through crossface or underhook dominance; second, neutralize the bottom player's ability to create angles by controlling their head and shoulder alignment; third, systematically remove their defensive structures (knee shield, lockdown, frames); and finally, complete the pass when they are flattened and immobilized. The biomechanical principle of creating a 'wedge' with your body position—where your chest drives into their upper body while your hips apply pressure to their lower body—creates the immobility necessary for high-percentage passing. Understanding that passing is not about speed but about creating a position where the opponent cannot move is the key distinction between effective and ineffective half guard passing.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, half guard passing is one of the most important skills because almost everyone will recover to half guard when you're working to pass their full guard or when they're escaping bad positions. I've built my entire passing game around being extremely comfortable and dominant in half guard passing positions. The key insight from high-level competition is that you need to have multiple passing solutions ready because good half guard players will defend differently. Some guys play knee shield and frames, others use lockdown, some immediately try to get underhooks and come up. You have to be able to recognize what they're doing and immediately apply the correct counter. My go-to sequence is establishing crossface control first, which shuts down about 70% of their options immediately. If they have knee shield, I smash it down and go to headquarters or knee slice. If they get underhook, I'm immediately attacking kimura or darce because that's when they're most vulnerable. The mental game is also critical—you have to be patient and not rush. I've seen so many matches where guys get impatient in half guard and get swept because they tried to force a pass that wasn't there. When you have proper control and pressure, the pass will come. The competition-proven reality is that systematic pressure beats dynamic movement almost every time in half guard passing at the highest levels.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Half guard passing in the 10th Planet system is all about understanding that you're in a dangerous position if you don't respect what the bottom player can do. We've developed the lockdown, electric chair, and deep half specifically to punish passers who use traditional pressure passing. So when I'm on top passing, I'm hyper-aware of lockdown threats and I'm constantly working to keep my trapped leg mobile and maintain the angle that prevents lockdown establishment. The innovative approach we use is the 'headquarters' concept where instead of trying to smash through immediately, you establish a stable position with your knee cutting through their knee shield while maintaining crossface control. From there, you're in a position where you can attack submissions (kimura, darce), complete the pass, or take the back depending on their reactions. What a lot of guys don't realize is that half guard passing isn't just about getting to side control—it's about creating dilemmas where every defensive reaction opens up a different attack. If they try to retain guard, you have passing options. If they try to sweep, you have submission entries. The creative element is using leg weaves and hip switches to stay one step ahead of their recovery attempts. In no-gi especially, you can't rely on just pressure because good guys will slip out, so you need dynamic passing entries combined with strategic pressure application. The 10th Planet methodology teaches that half guard passing is actually one of the best positions to attack from if you understand the system.
